item.title: Streeting prepares to resign and challenge Starmer for Labour leadership
item.description: Health Secretary Wes Streeting is preparing to resign from the cabinet as early as Thursday to mount a formal leadership challenge against Prime Minister Keir Starmer, according to a report in The Times. The move, which would represent the most direct threat yet to Starmer's premiership, came after Streeting held a brief meeting with the Prime Minister on Wednesday morning ahead of the King's Speech.

item.title: Australia joins UK-France naval mission to secure Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
The United Kingdom and France hosted a multinational meeting of defense ministers on Tuesday to advance plans for a naval mission to protect commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, as Australia confirmed it would join the effort and Britain deployed a warship to the region.

UK Defence Secretary John Healey and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin co-chaired the virtual meeting, which brought together representatives from more than 40 countries to discuss military contributions to the European-led coalition. The talks came as Iran issued sharp warnings against any foreign naval presence in the waterway.

item.title: Truck convoys across Arabia become lifeline amid Hormuz closure
item.description:
Convoys of heavy-duty trucks barreling across the Arabian desert have become an unlikely escape valve for the global economy, as the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz forces Gulf states to improvise new land routes for energy and commodity shipments, according to a report published Monday by The Wall Street Journal.

The truck convoys represent one piece of a broader scramble by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Oman to keep trade flowing more than two months after Iran effectively shut down the world's most important oil chokepoint in late February, in retaliation for U.S. and Israeli strikes. Before the closure, roughly 20 million barrels of crude oil passed through the strait daily. Traffic has since collapsed to about 5% of pre-war levels, according to maritime data firm Kpler.

item.title: Iran says Hormuz control could double its oil revenues
item.description: Iranian Army Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia declared on Wednesday that Tehran's strategic grip over the Strait of Hormuz could generate revenues exceeding twice the country's oil income, as Iran deepens its efforts to formalize control over the world's most vital oil chokepoint amid its ongoing war with the United States and Israel.

item.title: Trump arrives in Beijing for summit with Xi amid Iran war tensions
item.description:
President Donald Trump touched down in Beijing on Wednesday for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, arriving against the backdrop of a fragile ceasefire in the Iran conflict and deep uncertainty over whether the two superpowers can find common ground on the Middle East, trade, and Taiwan.

The visit — the first by a U.S. president to China since Trump's own trip in November 2017 — had originally been scheduled for late March but was postponed due to the outbreak of war with Iran in late February. Trump was greeted with a red-carpet welcome ceremony, with Chinese and American flags waved in rhythmic unison by uniformed greeters, according to the Associated Press. The formal bilateral talks between Trump and Xi are set to begin Thursday and extend through Friday.

item.title: Moscow bans media from publishing drone strike aftermath
item.description: Moscow's city government has prohibited the publication of photos, videos, and text describing the aftermath of drone strikes and what officials termed "terrorist attacks," extending a pattern of information control that has spread across more than 30 Russian regions since 2025.

item.title: UAE denies Netanyahu's claimed secret visit during Iran war
item.description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office announced on Wednesday that he had secretly traveled to the United Arab Emirates during the Israel-U.S. war with Iran and met with UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Al-Ain on March 26, describing the encounter as an "historic breakthrough" in bilateral relations. Hours later, the UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a flat denial, calling any such reports "entirely unfounded."

item.title: Rutte proposes NATO allies spend 0.25% of GDP on Ukraine aid annually
item.description:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has proposed that all 32 alliance members commit to spending 0.25% of their gross domestic product each year to support Ukraine, a plan that could nearly triple collective aid to roughly $143 billion annually, according to Politico.

Rutte floated the idea at a closed meeting of NATO ambassadors in late April as the alliance prepares for its summer summit in Ankara, Turkey, scheduled for July 7–8. The proposal seeks to put Ukraine support on a more stable and predictable footing while narrowing the gap between high-contributing nations in northern Europe and less generous allies in the south.

item.title: Trump, Xi open landmark summit in Beijing with calls for cooperation
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping opened a closely watched bilateral summit at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on Thursday, exchanging a formal handshake and warm remarks as the leaders of the world's two largest economies sought to project cooperation amid deep divisions over trade, technology, and the war in Iran.

The meeting marks the first visit by a sitting U.S. president to China in nearly nine years, since Trump's own 2017 trip during his first term. Originally planned for April, the summit was postponed due to the U.S. and Israeli military campaign in Iran.

item.title: Russia's massive drone attack forces Slovakia to briefly shut Ukraine border
item.description: Slovakia shut down all border crossings with Ukraine on Wednesday afternoon after Russian attack drones struck the western Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod, located just kilometers from the Slovak frontier. The closures, which lasted roughly two hours, came as Russia launched what Ukrainian officials described as one of the largest aerial assaults since the start of the full-scale invasion.

item.title: Xi warns Trump of conflict risk if Taiwan is mishandled
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered a pointed warning to President Donald Trump on Thursday during their summit in Beijing, saying the two countries risk "clashes and even conflicts" if the Taiwan issue is mishandled, according to a readout published by the official Xinhua news agency.

Xi told Trump that if Taiwan is handled well, US-China relations "will enjoy overall stability," but that failure to do so would put "the entire relationship in great jeopardy," calling Taiwan the "most important issue in China-US relations," according to state broadcaster CCTV.

The warning stood in sharp contrast to Trump's warm public remarks at the Great Hall of the People, where the US president told Xi, "You're a great leader. Sometimes people don't like me saying it, but I say it anyway, because it's true." He added, "It's an honor to be with you. It's an honor to be your friend," and predicted the bilateral relationship would be "better than ever before," the Associated Press reported.

item.title: Iran demands BRICS condemn US-Israel war at Delhi summit
item.description: Foreign ministers from BRICS nations opened a two-day meeting in New Delhi on Thursday, with the war in Iran launched by the United States and Israel on February 28 dominating the agenda and laying bare fractures within the expanded bloc. The gathering at Bharat Mandapam, chaired by Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, brings together diplomats from the group's 11 member states — including Iran, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia, countries on opposing sides of the Middle East conflict.

item.title: Streeting resigns as health secretary, launches bid to unseat Starmer
item.description:
Wes Streeting resigned as Britain's Health Secretary on Thursday, throwing down a direct challenge to Prime Minister Keir Starmer's leadership of the Labour Party and plunging the governing party deeper into crisis following its disastrous local election results last week.

The BBC confirmed Streeting's resignation on Thursday morning, capping days of speculation after allies had spent Wednesday night phoning Labour MPs to drum up support for a formal leadership contest. The move came just a day after Streeting held a tense, 16-minute meeting with Starmer at Downing Street, following which the Prime Minister insisted he had "full confidence" in his Health Secretary.

item.title: Samsung begins cutting chip output ahead of historic strike
item.description:
Samsung Electronics has begun reducing semiconductor production ahead of a planned 18-day general strike set to begin on May 21, after marathon government-mediated negotiations collapsed without a deal. The company started cutting chip output on Thursday, according to MoneyToday, as more than 50,000 union workers prepare for what would be the first full shutdown of Samsung's chip fabrication lines in 42 years.

The move comes one day after South Korea's Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol warned that a strike "must not happen under any circumstances," calling it a threat to the country's economic growth, exports, and financial markets. Prime Minister Kim Min-seok convened an emergency meeting of ministers and pledged to "actively support labor-management dialogue so that this does not lead to a strike under any circumstances".

item.title: US clears 10 Chinese firms for Nvidia H200 chips, but no deliveries made
item.description:
The U.S. Commerce Department has approved roughly 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia H200 artificial intelligence chips, but not a single delivery has taken place, Reuters reported on Thursday, leaving a multibillion-dollar technology deal in limbo as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang seeks a breakthrough during President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

The approved buyers include Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and JD.com, with distributors such as Lenovo and Foxconn also cleared to act as intermediaries, according to three people familiar with the matter. Each approved customer can purchase up to 75,000 chips under U.S. licensing terms. Lenovo confirmed to Reuters that it "is one of several companies approved to sell H200 in China as part of Nvidia's export license".

item.title: Webb telescope spots most primitive galaxy ever found
item.description:
An international team of astronomers has used the James Webb Space Telescope to characterize the most chemically primitive star-forming galaxy ever observed — an ultra-faint speck of light from 13 billion years ago whose oxygen content is just 1/240th that of the Sun.

The findings, published in Nature on May 13, detail how the team achieved a definitive characterization of the galaxy known as LAP1-B, located at a redshift of 6.625, placing it roughly 800 million years after the Big Bang during the epoch of reionization. The discovery provides what scientists describe as a direct ancestral link to the mysterious "fossil galaxies" found orbiting the Milky Way today.

item.title: About 30 vessels cross Strait of Hormuz with Iran's approval amid standoff
item.description:
Approximately 30 vessels have transited the Strait of Hormuz with Tehran's authorization since Wednesday, Iran's state television reported on Thursday, marking a notable uptick in maritime traffic through the contested waterway even as negotiations to end the war remain stalled.

An official from the naval branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps told the broadcaster that Iran's stance toward "hostile ships" remains unchanged and that such vessels would not be allowed passage. The IRGC continues to require all vessels to obtain approval before transiting the strait, a practice formalized in recent weeks through Tehran's newly established Persian Gulf Strait Authority.

item.title: Iran war could cost US $300 billion, analysis warns
item.description:
The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran — now in its eleventh week — is threatening to deliver a $300 billion economic shock, as disruptions to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz continue to drive up energy, food, and transportation costs worldwide, according to a MarketWatch analysis published on Tuesday.

The warning comes as new U.S. inflation data showed consumer prices rose 3.8 percent in April compared to a year earlier, the fastest pace since May 2023, fueled largely by surging energy costs tied to the conflict. Average fuel prices in the United States have climbed 55 percent since the war began on February 28, with 80 percent of Americans now saying higher gasoline prices are burdening their household finances, according to an NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll.

item.title: ICC-wanted senator flees Philippine Senate after gunfire
item.description: Philippine Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of crimes against humanity, escaped the Senate building early Thursday after a dramatic standoff that saw gunfire erupt inside the legislative chamber, sending journalists and staff scrambling for cover.

item.title: Trump says Xi pledged no arms for Iran, help on Hormuz
item.description: President Trump said Thursday that Chinese President Xi Jinping offered Beijing's assistance in reopening the Strait of Hormuz and committed that China would not supply military equipment to Iran, characterizing the pledges as a diplomatic win following a two-day summit in Beijing.
